The actual funds to make a game are generally orders of magnitude higher than can be obtained through crowdfunding alone for a truly polished and fully developed large game.

There are a couple of angles to this:

--1) A development studio without any other investments means their success translates directly into their profits and their intellectual property is completely their own. This creates a direct relationship between customers and developers, which is beneficial.

--2) A studio that secures a publisher after the crowdfunding campaign and some development time has passed means they are in a better position to negotiate. With a publisher, you can expect to have more funds available and support in case there are any mistakes, along with a substantial marketing engine at their disposal. It also increases the overall project development time, which might not be ideal for the impatient but is good overall for the quality and polish of the project.

We have all seen the issues with large crowdfunding projects that almost but do not quite reach their full potential (except for one notable case that was simply poorly managed). Especially when looking at their expansion packs.

You need time to test and refine mechanics, as well as rewrite and edit text and redo levels.

The mixed results of one project suggest that about 50% of its quality was lost mainly due to development time. Costs have decreased, but in the past, a project of the same size would have had significantly more in development funds, and it shows.

--3) A studio that already has a publisher. At first glance, this may seem like a marketing strategy, and it *pretty much is*, with publishers looking to gauge interest in a project and essentially secure what amounts to guaranteed pre-orders.

**Nevertheless**, it has some pretty **huge** implications.

Publishers and investors are not inherently bad; **every other medium has publishers** and they often work well with creators (except in some areas). So it is not a bad thing in itself.

The problem lies in the **current form** of the gaming industry and its biggest faults: budget and demographics.

Currently, publishers and their large studios only target a specific, albeit large, demographic to the exclusion of everything else, implementing absolutely astronomical budgets in their pursuit and maximum exploitation to recoup costs. This is a misguided approach, and they need to change.

This type of crowdfunding is the first step in the evolution of publishers moving more towards a Hollywood model. The issues with publishers are the reason crowdfunding was created and became so successful, so they finally got the message and are starting to adapt.

Although publishers using crowdfunding may seem somewhat clumsy, and it is, it is a significant step towards the future.

--4) **Now on to some less favorable implications**. The pool of crowdfunding money is limited, and all three instances are very much in competition. It is a zero-sum game. Publishers have the potential to overwhelm the system with marketing while still failing to understand demographics and budgets, which can destabilize the system.

While large projects may benefit from publishers/investors, smaller scoped projects are often right on target for budget and development. One project with its budget was pretty much spot on and realized its potential. Thus, shrinking the available funds would be a loss.

Since publishers do not care much about the money generated from crowdfunding and only care about the interest, it would be better to have a separate system and leave the funding pool to those who truly need it.

Level design, character design, writing, and art are quite different from game design, which focuses on game mechanics, systems of feedback, and learning.

For game design specifically, what you **absolutely need** is a game design binder, a notebook, or a tool to keep track of your concepts, patterns, and analysis of other games (I use a digital organizational tool). Create as many game projects as you can, add your thoughts, imagine how they work, and collect ideas for them.

Do not worry about which mechanics work or don't work; you do not even have to prototype. What you are looking for is to have the greatest possibility space for solutions. Embrace the chaos through which creativity is born.

Those who rush straight to prototyping and iteration often lack a solid foundation and are going in blind.

However, prototyping is still valuable, so the best tools for it are components for tabletop games like dice, cards, chess pieces, tokens, and so on.

I wish there was a good prototyping tool. I think the best one right now is a 3D tabletop game platform that is commonly used in streams, but I haven't tested it.

The practice of a game designer is not prototyping but game analysis. Prototyping is for verification, but before you can do that, you need something to verify. It is pointless to prototype if you have very little conceptual knowledge to verify. It is also unproductive to seek that conceptual knowledge through trial and error when there are other sources that have already done that for you. That is why you analyze games before you prototype and iterate.

For example, when I start my day, I always have my organizational tool open in my browser.  
When I watch or read an article, I summarize it and add my thoughts to my notes.  
When I watch a gameplay video (especially by expert players), I add my thoughts on it.  
When I get an idea for a game, I write it down and see what kind of games are similar to it, collecting ideas from other games that would work with it.  
And so on...

Prototyping is done only when I take an idea seriously; otherwise, random musings are fine.

Also, since prototyping is for verification, it’s important to be thorough in writing the prototyping report, including the context, why it works, and why it doesn't. Just because it does not work in that particular instance does not mean it will never work in all cases. Verification is a powerful tool that can be misused.

**Open World RTS** is an intriguing concept to explore that might address some of the issues currently faced by the genre.

With the emphasis on competitive elements and micromanagement in RTS games, much of the enjoyment has been diminished. What RTS games used to offer were engaging campaigns with puzzle-like maps that explored various aspects of resources and units, allowing players to plan and target enemy weaknesses.

Open World games provide the freedom to approach challenges at one's own pace.

I believe the ideal format for an Open World RTS would be a campaign lasting around 8-20 hours on a relatively large map, but not infinite, featuring seeded resources and enemy placements, along with a more passive AI and a clear objective to achieve.

Players shouldn't necessarily have to lose, and at easier difficulty levels, they wouldn't need to worry about being actively hunted or facing a time limit to accomplish their goals.

For my game idea, I will draw inspiration from games like a resource management game that could already be considered an Open World RTS but lacks significant enemy opposition. The logistics, resource management, and base building elements are precisely what we want. Another game has fascinating unit design and a campaign structure centered around a race for resources to escape a doomed planet, which aligns with the objectives we seek. It also features underground layers with interesting strategic properties. A space-themed game offers various abilities, units, and mechanics, while another game is known for its mech and weapon design, along with impressive aesthetics and destruction.

In this scenario, let's say the goal is to construct a large spaceship that requires controlling 70% of the map's resources, while the enemy is also building a spaceship that you must sabotage to prevent its completion. Players can research and build components for their ship, culminating in an ultimate showdown between the two forces.

A significant challenge in RTS games, particularly in an Open World setting, is the potential for creating an invincible super-powered force that could dominate everything. To address this, we need some concepts.

Static defenses can **effectively defeat** mobile forces but are vulnerable to logistical attacks and infiltration.  
Mobile forces are also limited in terms of the types of units they can deploy and can be detected, triggering alerts.  
Any given area has a finite amount of resources and stockpiles for creating new units, ammunition, and energy, which require periodic supplies that can be raided.  
Transports and mobile defenses are also constrained.

With this framework, players have a wide range of options to approach specific locations. They can infiltrate stealthily and sabotage key locations to weaken defenses enough to deploy their forces. They can skirmish and raid supply lines to disrupt repairs and gradually starve the enemy. Continuous harassment will prompt the enemy to deploy mobile forces to defend their supply routes, giving them the advantage of static defenses in that area.

**As an attacker, your advantage** lies in analyzing enemy placements and planning to bring the right forces for the task. The enemy's setup is like a puzzle to solve. You could invest maximum forces and resources, but even then, you would be limited, racing to be as efficient as possible in the shortest time.

To facilitate this, there are several broad concepts to consider.

#### Artillery, Shields, Anti-Air, Underground, and Industry.

**Artillery** consists of large static defenses positioned on mountains with extensive ranges and trajectories. They are essentially devastating weapons. Any large vehicles or formations are vulnerable if detected and within range. You can attack with numerous smaller units, but that makes you susceptible to conventional defenses and enemy mobile forces. Artillery in a valley can present a significant challenge, while traversing mountains is only feasible for smaller units and air vehicles.

Artillery on flat ground is less effective, as it can be more easily targeted and has a severely limited range.

**Shield generators** protect areas from particle and laser weapons but do not affect projectiles or unit mobility. Particle weapons can be powerful with long ranges. Some special large vehicles have shield generators, but they are less effective than static ones.

**Anti-Air** consists of powerful lasers that can eliminate all air vehicles within a wide range. Air vehicles are intentionally designed to have limited effectiveness in this game.

**Underground** routes can bypass all defenses, including artillery, but require substantial logistical support. They are vulnerable to mobile forces, as they can easily become bottlenecked due to the structure of corridors and have strict limits on the size of units that can enter. They can lead to labyrinthine warfare, with many passages created. They can also serve as ambush points, resource stockpiles, and secret bases. Tunnels can be collapsed with explosives over a limited area. There are four height levels corresponding to plain, hill, valley, and mountain. Rivers are inaccessible at the underground level, and bodies of water at the plain level are strictly off-limits through underground routes.

**Industry** involves a system of industrialization, resource harvesting, and transportation, transforming resources into parts, components, buildings, and ultimately mobile forces. These are areas set up for construction, research, and defense.

To facilitate logistics, players can **create train tracks and roads using special vehicles** that automatically construct paths on the map. Players can then build the trains and vehicles needed to transport resources, supplies, and units. The tracks and roads are indestructible (as they would be trivial to repair), but bridges and tunnels are vulnerable. Trains and roads can be constructed up to the valley height level and require tunnels to traverse beyond the mountain height level.

Players can also establish specialized industrial areas for military purposes as part of the base for that zone, processing that zone's resources to be sent back to more developed industrial bases.

#### Unit and Vehicle Designs and Sizes:

**Troops and small mechs** are designed for infiltration, high mobility, and terrain traversal, equipped with jetpacks and grappling hooks, allowing them to utilize environmental cover for protection. They can plant explosives but are vulnerable to heavy firepower.

When uploading the challenge, they can also perform further editing and scripting to refine it.

**Players would compete against setups from other players that have achieved victory.**

Players would start small with a safe timer during which they can develop freely without challenge, along with some initial resources. Their technology would be basic until they acquire more unique resources by raiding enemy-controlled areas and reverse engineering enemy technology. The enemy would initially control the map with all their structures in place, but their development would be paused until the safety timer expires. After that, the enemy will gradually develop their spaceship, but as the player gains control of more of the map, the balance will eventually shift in favor of the player. Resources would be organized in tiers, with more basic and common resources being more readily available. **Emergence boiled down is just a combination explosion.**

There is nothing "unintentional" about it; there is no magic, and the developer does not have to be blind and make funky rituals to achieve it.

It's systems interacting with systems.

How it works is a system generates some state (possibility space).

If two systems interact, then their state multiplies together: state X state.

Pile up the systems, and you can get:   
state X state X state X state X state ==> A combination explosion.

Why is it called a combination explosion? If we give every system a concrete number of states like 100, then:

100 X 100 X 100 X 100 X 100 == 10,000,000,000 possible states when combined.

Now all of this is not all fun since finding systems that interact well with each other and ensuring that nothing goes horribly wrong is hard work. The most likely cases in which you find this are inspired by real-world engineering like circuitry and physics simulation.

While we are at it, the definition of **depth** in games is also easy to define. If the **complexity** of the game is the total amount of possibility space (the above number of states), then **depth** is just the amount of **viable** possibility space. What **viable** means is that it has some uses in a particular context so that if the player chooses it, they would be better off in reaching their goal in winning or achieving an objective. In other words, their decisions are meaningful (the whole saying "games are a series of interesting decisions"). How you make the possibility space is through **balancing** the various strategies, systems, units, builds, and playstyles between each other; **it's all hard work and no shortcuts**.

Furthermore, increasing the possibility space can actually decrease the viable possibility space by making available **degenerate strategies** that are better than any other strategy, thus it is no longer a choice.

Additionally, in a **non-competitive** game, you can sidestep degenerate strategies as long as they can be excluded in some form. There is a so-called **difficulty threshold** that corresponds to the number of viable strategies as long as the player has a way to exclude always playing the degenerate strategies. In other words, you can get **replayability** of the game through **exploring** different **builds**.

In these non-competitive games with a set difficulty threshold, you can focus on more **free-form exploration** and **player ingenuity** and **creativity**.

A well-known action RPG is the best example of exploring different builds; they have set difficulty challenges in which the different builds are viable. Furthermore, with a resource system that still values lower-tiered rewards for a shared account, the builds do not have to reach the highest level of difficulty and can be satisfied in their role at lower levels.

A popular card game is the best example of **failing this** since, while you have the option of creating various decks, it is a **competitive game**, thus what is **viable is set** into a limited number of **meta decks**.

Changing the systems and factors through patches and expansions that affect the viable possibility space is what is referred to as **changing the meta**.

You can create a **slice** of a city centered around a point of interest like a market district, with suggestions that there may be more elements beyond what is accessible. 

A great example of this is a popular role-playing game where the urban environments feel alive, even if the maps are ultimately constrained.
